brooklyn.intro: Bedford-Stuyvesant and Brooklyn CORE: garbage, construction jobs, and the institutions and political power people built for themselves.
brooklyn.critique: The intro promises garbage, housing and construction jobs, but no stop covers the garbage protest or the 1963 construction-site campaign. The CORE stop is an event introduction about David Dennis in Mississippi, not about Brooklyn at all. The Randolph Evans quote is a garbled auto-caption about a police killing outside the unit's stated themes, and two quotes stop mid-sentence.

stops.note: Brian Purnell on Brooklyn CORE's 1963 protests at the Downstate Medical Center construction site against discrimination in the building trades.
stops.quote: Thousands of demonstrators from around the city participate in this pretty consistently throughout July of 1963. By the end of August, over 800 people are arrested by doing things such as this, lying down in front of work sites, blocking cement trucks … to call attention to their demand.

stops.note: A panelist on the Bedford-Stuyvesant Restoration Corporation, one of the first community development corporations, and its roots in women-led mutual aid.
stops.quote: But their idea was that you would combine retail businesses, services, manufacturing. You would channel the profits from these back into the community in the forms of jobs, of decent housing, and improved social services that were sort of under the control and direction of people in the community themselves.

stops.note: Brian Purnell on Brooklyn CORE dumping Bedford-Stuyvesant's uncollected garbage at Borough Hall, and what integration meant in Brooklyn.
stops.quote: Show us integration with better sanitation is one of the placards that they held, which I think is interesting because it shows again what integration means in a place like Brooklyn. It's not about sitting next to someone in a cafe or a restaurant.

stops.note: One of the filmmakers of The Sun Rises in the East on the East, a Pan-African cultural organization that built a school, jazz club and food co-op in Bed-Stuy.
stops.quote: The East created over a dozen institutions in Bed-Stuy. … They had a school, they had a jazz club, they opened up a food co-op in the 70s in Brooklyn.

stops.note: Historian Anastasia Curwood on Shirley Chisholm representing Bedford-Stuyvesant in the New York State Assembly before her 1968 election to Congress.
stops.quote: She represented Bedford-Stuyvesant in Brooklyn, the 17th Assembly District. And while she was in the State Assembly, she was advocating for expanded abortion rights or a liberalization of abortion laws, minimum wage and worker protections for domestic workers, like her mother had been.

culture.intro: Music, dance, theater and the Black Arts Movement as part of the struggle, and who gets to archive them.
culture.critique: Every quote broke off mid-sentence, several just as the point arrived (Woodard ends on 'Daddy', the theater quote on 'A part'). The Erica Edwards stop is about US imperial culture in general rather than Black arts as part of the struggle, and the Papua New Guinea quote is garbled and thin. The Black Arts Movement, one of the unit's two topics, had only that one passing stop, and dance was missing.

stops.note: A panelist at the 2010 conference on the Great Migration as the start of a Black cultural revolution, beginning with the shift from spirituals to gospel.
stops.quote: And that Black exodus causes a Black cultural revolution as people are moving. … There's a fight that goes on in the Black churches from going from spiritual music to gospel music. It's a profound change in the ethos of Black spiritual awakening.

stops.note: Hanif Abdurraqib on how Ohio funk and unrecorded Delta blues made him ask who gets to archive and name their own musical history.
stops.quote: I began seeing through music and thinking about through music who gets an opportunity to archive and who gets to self-determine their own archive, and through that self-determination who gets to name their own archive and who gets to name the importance they had in the world.

stops.note: Tammy Brown on Trinidad-born choreographer Pearl Primus as a bridge from the Harlem Renaissance to the Black Arts Movement, with dance as a weapon.
stops.quote: She is really, I argue, the bridge between the Harlem Renaissance and the Black Arts Movement … she was the first Black person to integrate the New Dance Group, and their model was dance as a weapon for social change.

stops.note: A panelist at the Malcolm X centennial on how Malcolm's assassination sent Larry Neal uptown and helped start the Black Arts Movement in Harlem.
stops.quote: One of the founders of the Black Arts Movement, Larry Neal, who was a prolific writer, playwright, and critic, was in the audience when Brother Malcolm was martyred. … And as a result of Malcolm's martyrdom, he moved up to Harlem because he wanted to be closer to his people.

stops.note: A theater historian on the panel on how Alice Childress's Trouble in Mind and Baldwin's Blues for Mister Charlie turned the gaze back on white audiences.
stops.quote: What Alice Childress, in her play, particularly Trouble in Mind, does, and what Baldwin does in plays like Blues for Mr. Charlie, is to turn the camera to white people and say, hey, let me show you yourself.

faith.intro: Churches as organizing spaces, radicals who reconciled faith with Marxism, and Black women who fought for their rights inside the church.
faith.critique: The moments were apt, but the quotes began mid-sentence and stopped before their point. The Murch quote ended before saying churches housed the survival programs, the Ford quote before religion entered the story, and the Wimbush quote mid-letter. The Abyssinian stop misheard Adam Clayton Powell as 'Adder Clinton College'. The 2016 stop quoted a garbled fragment about Hedgeman rather than the Powell Sr. passage on the church. The intro left out Black women fighting inside the church, which the 2024 stop is about.

stops.note: A panelist on how labor radical Vicki Garvin, as a young woman in 1930s Harlem, came to protest through Abyssinian Baptist Church.
stops.quote: She became active with the Abyssinian Baptist Church, which her parents had joined when they moved to Harlem. … It was actually through Adam Clayton Powell she participated in the first protest around the Don't Buy Where You Can't Work program.

stops.note: Donna Murch (Living for the City) on finding that the Black Panther Party's breakfast and survival programs were housed in Black churches.
stops.quote: A surprise that I also found from doing research is that many of the breakfast programs and the different survival programs of the party were located in local Black churches. … And in much of the North, it's churches that actually provided the infrastructure for the Panther survival programs.

stops.note: From a short excerpt of a 2016 panel on the church and the struggle: a panelist quotes Abyssinian's Adam Clayton Powell Sr. on what the church is for.
stops.quote: The question now is what is the church doing for the amelioration of the condition of mankind? … The chief work of the church is not to get men and women ready to die but to get men and women ready to live.

stops.note: Melissa Ford (A Brick and a Bible) on 1930s Black Communists in the Midwest rewriting spirituals to bring Marxism into the language of faith.
stops.quote: We hear them using old African-American spirituals but changing the lyrics. So we have that Give Me That Old-Time Religion, which is an old spiritual, but they change the lyrics to … it was good enough for Comrade Lenin and it's good enough for me.

stops.note: Dylan Penningroth on a 1966 letter in which church member Verita Wimbush planned a march on her bishop's house, and Black women's two-front war.
stops.quote: What Verita Wimbush is showing is that Black women were essentially fighting a two-front war. One was against white supremacy in society. … But they're also fighting a second war, and that's against male supremacy in church and in civil rights organizations.

gender.intro: Black feminist and queer organizing, Black queer life before Stonewall, HIV, the Free Joan Little campaign and the making of reproductive justice.
gender.critique: Most quotes were set-up rather than substance: Cooper Owens describes how she got into the field, Guy-Sheftall talks about archive access without saying anything about Coretta Scott King's LGBTQ solidarity, and the Joan Little quote is a filmmaker recalling where she was sitting. Reproductive justice was represented only by a personal origin story, never defined. None of the quotes began at a sentence start.

stops.note: Barbara Smith on her work in the 1970s, when almost nothing reflected Black feminist or queer women's lives and she and others built the field from scratch.
stops.quote: What I was doing during those years was to build Black feminism, to build a Black feminist movement, to fight homophobia particularly in Black context, to build Black women studies, particularly Black women's literature, because literature was my field.

stops.note: Loretta Ross on the 12 Black women who met in Chicago in June 1994 and coined reproductive justice, starting from white supremacy.
stops.quote: We centered ourselves in the lens, asking what we wanted from reproductive politics in this country. We started with the acknowledgment that if you don't understand white supremacy, everything else about reproductive politics will confuse you, because you simply do not understand how the socially engineered different reproductive destinies work.

stops.note: Steven Thrasher on how a CDC projection about HIV among Black gay men led him to the Missouri prosecution of Michael Johnson for HIV transmission.
stops.quote: A really alarming statistic came out from the CDC that one in every two Black gay men were projected to become HIV positive in our lifetime, and ended up going to Missouri to study the case of a young man named Michael Johnson who was being prosecuted for HIV transmission.

stops.note: Cookie Woolner (The Famous Lady Lovers) on Black women who loved women in the early 20th century and the lives they built long before Stonewall.
stops.quote: My book reveals the way that Black women who loved women, who again were known as often lady lovers or women lovers in the early 20th century, the ways they boldly created lives that allowed them the freedom to nurture queer relationships long before the Stonewall uprising of 1969.

stops.note: Christina Greene reads from Free Joan Little on the coalition that saw the 1974 killing of a white jailer as a Black woman's self-defense against rape.
stops.quote: Feminists of all kinds, Black power activists, prison abolitionists … and traditional civil rights leaders saw a victim of sexual violence and racism, a vulnerable Black woman who had valiantly defended herself against one of the age-old and unforgivable crimes of white supremacy.

harlem.intro: Harlem as a place of schools, churches, uprisings and campus fights, from the 1964 rebellion and the Morningside Park fight to Harlem Prep and Malcolm X's city.
harlem.critique: The opening quote is audience warm-up ('How many of you all live in Harlem?') and says nothing about Harlem's history, the Teachers Union stop is a table-of-contents list of book chapters, and the 1964 rebellion stop is a scholar describing his curiosity rather than the event. The intro promises churches, but no stop delivers one, and the Ethelred Brown church named in a note is never quoted.

stops.note: Michael Flamm, author of In the Heat of the Summer, on the July 1964 Harlem uprising after an off-duty police officer killed Black teenager James Powell.
stops.quote: In an effort to suppress the barrage of bottles and bricks that begin to fly down on the officers from the buildings in Central Harlem, the NYPD does something unprecedented in its history. It begins to fire warning or suppressing shots. We have no idea who gave the order.

stops.note: Tammy Brown, author of City of Islands, on Jamaican-born Unitarian minister Ethelred Brown, whose Harlem Community Church served as a Socialist Party forum.
stops.quote: I start with a lesser-known Caribbean intellectual, Ethelred Brown. He was a minister, a Unitarian reverend from Jamaica, and in his case his church in Harlem, the Harlem Community Church, ended up being … more successful as a Socialist Party forum than particularly as a religious gathering space.

stops.note: Stefan Bradley on Columbia and Barnard Black students in the 1968 Morningside Park fight, joining Harlem residents to stop the university taking the park.
stops.quote: But I also think about, of course, there in Harlem, students wanting to be relevant … asking what the community needed. And the community said, you can help us by preventing your university from taking up all the good green space in the area.

stops.note: The author of Mapping Malcolm, who grew up on Malcolm X Boulevard, on how Malcolm X's legacy is written into Harlem's streets and buildings.
stops.quote: I grew up on Malcolm X Boulevard my whole life, just a few blocks from Temple No. 7. … And so in so many ways, my young childhood was animated by Malcolm X's legacy, as it's inscribed in Harlem's built environment.

stops.note: Barry Goldenberg on Harlem Prep, a tuition-free alternative school that Harlem educators, families and students built in the late 1960s.
stops.quote: My book tells what I think is this really incredible, powerful story of a school, this alternative school in Central Harlem that was tuition free, was a de facto public school in Central Harlem at the time.

health.intro: Medical racism and the movements against it, from the Lincoln Hospital takeover and hospital closings to HIV, food as a weapon and segregated maternity care.
health.critique: Two of the five stops covered the same event (the Young Lords' Lincoln Hospital takeover), and every quote started mid-sentence and stopped before saying anything substantive: the Aumoithe quote ends on 'this rhetoric of' and the Lincoln film quote is throat-clearing. The unit's second topic, Food and Leisure, had no stop at all, and the fitness quote leaned on unexplained pronouns. The intro promised fitness, which is now traded for food as a movement weapon and HIV as a map of inequality.

stops.note: Johanna Fernández on the Young Lords' 1970 occupation of Lincoln Hospital in the Bronx, after months of collecting patient and worker grievances went unanswered.
stops.quote: They literally invade the hospital with white coats and they lock all of the doors and windows … and their purpose is to dramatize the horrific conditions of health under which poor Black and Puerto Rican people are being treated at the butcher shop of the Bronx.

stops.note: George Aumoithe on what he found in presidential library archives: 1970s 'hospital cost containment' as a cover for closing hospitals in Black and poor areas.
stops.quote: Hospital cost containment was this euphemism essentially for cost cutting. I found reams of white papers and memos discussing this process of how do we take away hospital care without it coming across as discriminatory or singling out a particular group.

stops.note: Steven Thrasher on reporting from Ferguson in 2014, where HIV cases, Black poverty and police violence showed up in the same places on the map.
stops.quote: So I started seeing that these maps developing, the same maps where you had new cases of HIV, cases of HIV moving on towards AIDS and AIDS deaths, concentrations of Black poverty and police violence were all happening in the same map space.

stops.note: Bobby J. Smith II (Food Power Politics) on how Mississippi movement participants answered the withholding of food with what he calls emancipatory food power.
stops.quote: Black people never find themselves being passive in times of social struggle … they were doing what I call emancipatory food power, where they were counter-weaponizing food as a way to address food being weaponized against them.

stops.note: Alison Parker, Terrell's biographer, on Mary Church Terrell's miscarriage, stillbirth and loss of a newborn in segregated hospitals, and what Harriet Washington calls medical apartheid.
stops.quote: So Terrell knew firsthand the bitter pain of many Black women who were suffering from disproportionately high rates of miscarriage and infant mortality. And this inadequate and segregated health care is what Harriet Washington calls medical apartheid. And it contributed to higher rates of infant mortality for Black infants.

icons.intro: Rethinking the most familiar figures: Rosa Parks's lifelong radicalism, King in the North, and Coretta Scott King's own politics.
icons.critique: The intro promises Coretta Scott King's own politics, but no stop is about her; the 2024 stop is Brandon Terry on Martin's sermons as resources against pessimism. The 2023 Parks stop is Jeanne Theoharis explaining why she wrote a biography, which says nothing about Parks's radicalism. Quotes started mid-sentence ('slavery and during reconstruction...', 'actually was and I had loved...') and the Richen quote stopped before reaching the Joan Little work it promised.

stops.note: Peniel Joseph on King in Marks, Mississippi, in February 1968, contrasting the 40 acres Black people never got with the free land whites received under the Homestead Act.
stops.quote: And then he compares that story to the Homestead Act and how European immigrants and American citizens were given millions of acres of free land … And then King fast forwards to the Great Society and says these are the same people telling you to pull yourselves up by your bootstraps.

stops.note: Jeanne Theoharis on Rosa Parks meeting Malcolm X in Detroit in 1963, when he came to give the Message to the Grassroots speech.
stops.quote: I've always loved the story of her and Malcolm X. They meet for the first time in 1963 because he wants to meet her. He's come to Detroit. He's going to give them what we now know as the Message to the Grassroots speech.

stops.note: SNCC veteran Gwendolyn Zoharah Simmons on Coretta Scott King opposing the Vietnam War publicly before Martin did.
stops.quote: I think it's already clear that both Dr. King and Mrs. Coretta Scott King were peace activists. Mrs. King was more out front in her advocacy for an end to the war in Vietnam than was Dr. King for quite a while.

stops.note: Jeanne Theoharis on how King of the North began: researching Los Angeles before the Watts uprising, she kept finding King there.
stops.quote: And I'm doing all this research and I keep finding Martin Luther King. … And he's there in 62 talking about police brutality after the murder of Ron Stokes. And he's there in May of 1963 saying LA is as segregated as Birmingham.

stops.note: Filmmaker Yoruba Richen on Parks's work against sexual violence, from investigating cases in the 1940s South to heading Detroit's Free Joan Little defense committee.
stops.quote: One of the things that I learned was her lifelong activism around advocating for Black women who experienced sexual violence from the 1940s. … When she found out about this case, she became head of the Free Joan Little Defense Committee in Detroit.

left.intro: Communists, Popular Front women and the radicals who carried their politics from the 1930s into Black Power.
left.critique: The intro promises Popular Front women, but only Vicki Garvin appears, and two of five stops are about Harry Haywood. The Robeson quote is a garbled, mid-sentence fragment about 1960s pop music rather than Robeson's own politics, and the faith stop quotes abstract talk about 'Black Marxism' instead of an actual 1930s radical. Every quote started mid-sentence and the Garvin quote kept the mishearings 'Heide McCarthyism' and 'Pew Act'.

stops.note: A panelist at the 2010 Want to Start a Revolution? conference on Vicki Garvin, a Communist labor leader whose activism outlasted McCarthyism.
stops.quote: So while she was in the party in McCarthyism, actually called before HUAC, had to testify … it didn't end her political activism. She continued to engage and be organized, and I think that narrative is often lost.

stops.topic: Communist Party and the Black Left
stops.note: A panelist on Harry Haywood, the Communist theorist pushed out of the CPUSA, becoming a mentor to the young founders of Soulbook and RAM in the 1960s.
stops.quote: And finally, Harry Haywood was one of their mentors. One of the essays they published was from Harry Haywood, who at that time had been kind of run out of the Communist Party USA, was living in exile in Mexico.

stops.note: Shana Redmond, author of Everything Man, on Paul Robeson's anti-fascism, from the Spanish Civil War to delivering We Charge Genocide to the UN in 1951.
stops.quote: So yes, he's, as I mentioned, known for having sung on the battlefield during the Spanish Civil War … but also his anti-fascist activism and work was present in 1951, where he handed to the representative at New York City's UN office a copy of We Charge Genocide.

stops.topic: Communist Party and the Black Left
stops.note: Melissa Ford (A Brick and a Bible) on Carrie Smith, a Baptist churchwoman who led Black women in the Communist-backed 1933 Funsten nut pickers' strike in St. Louis.
stops.quote: The day before the strike is called, she's on the steps of City Hall in St. Louis, and the story goes she's holding a brick in one hand and a Bible in the other, and she says, girls, if we stick together we cannot lose.

stops.topic: Communist Party and the Black Left
stops.note: Ashley Farmer on Queen Mother Audley Moore, whose life ran from Garvey's UNIA through the Communist Party to the Republic of New Afrika.
stops.quote: To follow her life is to take you through Marcus Garvey's UNIA. It's to take you through the Communist Party. … It's to take you through the Republic of New Afrika, all the way to, say, the Million Man March.

malcolm.intro: Malcolm X through his mother Louise Little and his Garveyite roots, his Harlem fight with the police, the prisoners and young radicals he drew in, and the myths that still cloud him.
malcolm.critique: Two of five stops (2016 and 2025) make the same point, that the autobiography underplays Louise Little's Garveyism, and the 2016 one is a short excerpt clip. The intro promises his New York years, but no stop is set in Harlem, while it leaves out the prison letter and the myths that the stops do cover. Every quote began mid-sentence or mid-word ('particularly with the speech of...', 'politics of Brother Malcolm...').

stops.note: A panelist on the influences behind the Revolutionary Action Movement (RAM), including young people drawn in by Malcolm X's speeches and activism in the early 1960s.
stops.quote: And many people on the streets of urban communities in the early 1960s were influenced by the Nation, particularly with the speech of Malcolm X, the activism of Malcolm X. A lot of young people beginning to resonate with that.

stops.note: Clarence Taylor on the 1957 Harlem police beating of Johnson X. Hinton, which Malcolm X and the Nation of Islam answered with protest and a lawsuit.
stops.quote: In this case here we see Malcolm X, this is in 1957, and it is the Johnson X. Hinton case. This is Johnson Hinton, a man who was beaten badly by the police. He was beaten so badly they had to put a metal plate in his head.

stops.note: Garrett Felber (Those Who Know Don't Say) on a letter from an incarcerated Muslim to Malcolm X about the support prisoners needed from outside.
stops.quote: There's this letter actually in the book that I write about where an incarcerated Muslim is writing to Malcolm X, and he uses this phrase. He says, the fighting man cannot win the war without the moral support of the home front.

stops.note: Peniel Joseph (The Sword and the Shield) on the twin myths that Malcolm X was simply pro-violence and only worth taking seriously in his last year.
stops.quote: I think there's two myths, strong myths about Malcolm and Martin, that really clouds us. One for Malcolm, it's a twin myth of that he is pro-violence, and also a myth that he is constrained by the Nation of Islam and he's only good his last year.

stops.note: Erik McDuffie at the Malcolm X centennial panel on his mother, Grenada-born Louise Langdon Little, and how she drew him to Garvey.
stops.quote: Louise going to Montreal, where she met her husband, Earl Little, became involved in the Garvey movement through her uncle, Edgerton Langdon. … How she was critical to cultivating the Black radical internationalist politics of Brother Malcolm, cultivating his interest in Garvey.

method.intro: Finding aids, census matching, FBI files, collecting drives and biography: how the scholars in these recordings found their sources, and what the archive leaves out.
method.critique: Every quote started mid-sentence and broke off before the method was described: the seminary quote stops before she says what she matched, and the Reddick quote ends on 'he turns to his'. The Woodard stop is about the series' founding, not how sources were found, and the intro promised scrapbooks that no stop delivered. All the sources were archival collections; nothing showed scholars prying records out of the government.

stops.note: Daina Ramey Berry on rewriting archive finding aids so that enslaved people mentioned in a family letter are described, not treated as an afterthought.
stops.quote: Instead of having an inventory that describes a letter between a husband and wife, but maybe the last paragraph is all about enslaved people, then what would it look like if you wrote that inventory from the perspective of the enslaved families that were discussed?

stops.note: Kabria Baumgartner on finding Black students in 19th-century female seminaries by matching enrollment lists against census records.
stops.quote: Seminary catalogs actually proved to be a real boon, because I was able to do the painstaking work of matching a list of enrolled students with federal and state census records in order to identify a student's racial background.

stops.note: A panelist on political repression on building an archive from FBI files through Freedom of Information Act requests, a nine-year wait.
stops.quote: The archive that I built was primarily from the Freedom of Information Act … I made my first Freedom of Information Act request in 2014, and the book came out in February of this year, so part of the process was just waiting for documents.

stops.note: Laura Helton on curator L. D. Reddick's World War II call through the Black press for people to save their letters and diaries and send them to the Schomburg.
stops.quote: He did not trust the federal record-keeping systems to tell that story. And so he turns to his kind of movement roots and he puts out this national call through the Black press, through Black organizations, and says to people, save everything. … And send them to the Schomburg Collection.

stops.note: Alison Parker on discovering there was no adult biography of Mary Church Terrell, only children's books, and deciding to write one.
stops.quote: And then I found out that there were no biographies of Terrell written for adults, although there were at least a dozen written for children and youth. And that's what started me on my path to being a biographer of Mary Church Terrell.

north.intro: The movement outside the South: segregation by neighborhood rather than by statute, and the organizers who made it visible in New York, Detroit, Boston and Cleveland.
north.critique: The intro promises New York, Detroit, Boston and Cleveland, but the stops never reach Detroit or Boston, and the Cleveland stop quotes only the moderator's question, not Barbara Smith's answer. Three quotes begin mid-sentence or with procedural talk (the 2010 opener announcing the program, the special education stop starting 'classes at this point'), and the Purnell quote opens with a line he is setting up to refute, so out of context it says the opposite of his argument.

stops.topic: Northern Civil Rights and Jim Crow North
stops.note: Brian Purnell, author of Fighting Jim Crow in the County of Kings, on why housing segregation in liberal New York looked invisible and how Brooklyn CORE exposed it.
stops.quote: There's no red-faced, pot-bellied, southern sheriff saying, you can't live here. … There's no whites only fountains and whites only rest signs on restaurants. That's not on Flatbush Avenue. But there is this very palpable and real segregation that exists.

stops.topic: Northern Civil Rights and Jim Crow North
stops.note: Clarence Taylor on Harlem councilman Benjamin Davis and William Patterson of the Civil Rights Congress, who framed police brutality in 1930s and 1940s New York as the North's lynching.
stops.quote: This is Benjamin Davis, who was a councilman in Harlem in the late 1930s and 1940s … It's Davis who pushes this notion that police brutality is northern lynching.

stops.topic: Northern Civil Rights and Jim Crow North
stops.note: Zebulon Vance Miletsky, author of Before Busing, on how Brown v. Board pointed attention at the South and away from Boston, where school segregation law began.
stops.quote: Brown versus Board dealt with South, and one thought that's the end of the question then, because the South was the place where racism dwelt. … There's that Boston sleight of hand again, drawing your attention away from the North and from Boston, which is actually really where it all started.

stops.topic: Northern Civil Rights and Jim Crow North
stops.note: Barbara Smith, who grew up under Jim Crow in Cleveland, on how the Northern movement fought housing, schools and jobs rather than voting rights.
stops.quote: In the North, Black people could vote. You might not have anybody to vote for, but the thing is, voting was not the focus in the North. … Housing, school segregation, jobs. And that's exactly what the Civil Rights Movement was doing in Cleveland.

stops.topic: Northern Civil Rights and Jim Crow North
stops.note: Law professor Michelle Adams, author of The Containment, on the 1970 Detroit school case, Milliken v. Bradley, and Jim Crow's Northern variation.
stops.quote: When people think about Jim Crow, they think about segregated water fountains. They think about Brown. They think about the South. They don't think so much about what happened in the North. And so we had a nationwide program and governmental policy of Jim Crow that had different regional variations.

panthers.intro: The Panthers and their allies from Oakland to Chicago to the South Bronx: armed patrols, survival programs, the Rainbow Coalition and the women who ran it all.
panthers.critique: The intro promises Chicago and the Rainbow Coalition, but no stop is set in Chicago, and the Rainbow Coalition appears only in a note. The Takeover quote is the filmmaker describing her own path into activism, not the Lincoln Hospital takeover, and the spiritual wellness stop opens on a chapter outline outside the intro's themes. The Young Lords and Murch quotes start mid-sentence or end before their point.

stops.note: Jakobi Williams on Fred Hampton's Rainbow Coalition in Chicago, and how the Panthers set up breakfast programs and clinics for allied groups.
stops.quote: And the reason these groups join forces with them is because the party has programs. … So they set up their breakfast programs, and then they set up these breakfast programs, these clinics, every single program the party had, they set them up for these other groups as well.

stops.note: Johanna Fernandez on the Young Lords as one of the most ethnically diverse organizations of the era, and part of Hampton's Rainbow Coalition.
stops.quote: The Young Lords was one of the most ethnically diverse organizations of the period. Approximately 25 percent of the organization was composed of Black Americans, another five to seven percent non-Puerto Rican Latinx folks, and then Puerto Ricans.

stops.note: Carol Anderson, author of The Second, on the Panthers' legal armed patrols of the police and the California gun law written to stop them.
stops.quote: The Panthers are determined to provide self-defense for that Black community, and they know the law. And so they come armed. They know how far away to stand from the police, and the police do not like it.

stops.note: Filmmaker Emma Francis-Snyder on Lincoln Hospital in the South Bronx, the condemned city hospital the Young Lords took over in her film Takeover.
stops.quote: The Lincoln Hospital was known for being awful. It had been condemned by the city in 1945 and yet was the main city hospital for Puerto Ricans, migrants and immigrants in the South Bronx neighborhood.

stops.note: Suzanne Cope, author of Power Hungry, on Panther women like Cleo Silvers who ran the Free Breakfast for Children and other survival programs.
stops.quote: And so women were very instrumental in running these programs … And I know these are mostly, or pretty much all pictures of men. And I asked Cleo about that and she said, first of all, we were too busy working to have our picture taken.

police.intro: A long history of police violence and the fight against it, from 1930s Harlem to counterinsurgency abroad and reform at home.
police.critique: The intro opens with 1930s Harlem, but no stop covers it, and the 2017 stop is Clarence Taylor's garbled personal confession ('just German I'm old enough...') rather than a usable account of a case. The 2023 Burden-Stelly stop is an abstract claim that broke off mid-sentence and adds little beside the Schrader and Lytle Hernández stops. Every quote began mid-sentence, and the Schrader quote ended before his own argument about counterinsurgency.

stops.note: Michael Flamm (In the Heat of the Summer) on the protests after an off-duty police lieutenant killed Black teenager James Powell in July 1964, and their demand for civilian review.
stops.quote: The demonstrators have two core demands. The first is that they want Lieutenant Gilligan either suspended or fired from the force. The second thing they want is the creation of a true civilian review board with the majority of civilians on the board.

stops.note: Kelly Lytle Hernández (City of Inmates) on finding that Los Angeles police targeted Black residents only once Black LA grew large and concentrated.
stops.quote: The policing of Black folks did not begin until the rise of Black LA. So as long as our population was small, as long as our population was not concentrated and a threat to the white settler city, we really were not aggressively policed.

stops.note: Stuart Schrader (Badges Without Borders) argues US police were built for use at home and abroad at once, united by Cold War counterinsurgency.
stops.quote: Actually, our police systems have been designed and developed for deployment both at home and abroad simultaneously. And the argument I make is that the mission that unites the two, meaning home and abroad, is what I would call counterinsurgency.

stops.note: Anne Gray Fischer (The Streets Belong to Us) on the history of sexual policing of women, from Prohibition to broken windows policing in the 1980s.
stops.quote: My book is a history of sexual policing, or the state targeting and legal control of people's bodies in their presumed sexual activities. I'm looking at the enforcement of prostitution-related misdemeanors mostly between Prohibition in the 1920s to the rise of broken windows policing … in the 1980s.

stops.note: Shannon King (The Politics of Safety) on Harlem after the 1935 uprising, when residents described the police as an army of occupation.
stops.quote: One Black Harlemite wrote to the Black weekly calling for the community to protest "the presence of what can be called a police army of occupation for which I can see no real necessity." … I was surprised because this is the language that Black Power activists used in the 1960s.

power.intro: Black Power beyond its myths: its roots in Jim Crow, its reading movement, its feminists and its economics.
power.critique: The intro promises Black Power's local economics, but no stop covers economics. The Onaci stop starts mid-sentence on what students were told and never reaches his self-determination point. Several quotes are setups that stop before their payoff: Burgin's opens 'the myth that...' without listing the myths, and the Flo Kennedy quote lists party names rather than showing women's role in Black Power.

stops.note: Sherie Randolph on Flo Kennedy and the women who did the organizing work behind the 1967 Black Power Conference but are missing from its photographs.
stops.quote: What you don't see in this picture are all the women … who are actually running the meetings, doing the press, sending out pamphlets and actually making a lot of connections and building out this movement.

stops.note: A historian of the Oakland Panthers on where Black Power came from: Jim Crow, Black radical traditions and global revolution, but homegrown.
stops.quote: Black power was born out of the savagery of Jim Crow. It was born out of the ideological legacy of black non-conformists, the nationalists, the feminists, the anti-capitalists. It was born out of the possibility and influence of global revolution. It was internationalist, but it was not foreign.

stops.note: A panelist from The Economics of Black Power on federal and corporate economic development money after the uprisings and what it was really for.
stops.quote: I don't actually think that money was ever intended to get to any particular group. I think that money was intended to stop urban uprisings, to defang the black power movement, and to really divide the community.

stops.note: A panelist rereading H. Rap Brown's Die Nigger Die as part of a Black Power reading movement of bookstores and autobiographies.
stops.quote: The Black Freedom Movement was undergirded by an intellectual shift that saw both Black bookstores and Black literature on the upsurge. It was a reading movement. People informed themselves of the ideas and people wrote their stories.

stops.note: The author of Organizing Your Own, a Detroit study, on teaching Black Power through the myths that surround it.
stops.quote: How I teach the Black Power movement is really through the mythologies that surround it. So the idea that it was helplessly violent, that it was incredibly macho, that it was this serious break with the civil rights movement, and then always the idea that it was somehow anti-white.

prisons.intro: Mass incarceration as a long project: Attica's aftermath, women behind bars, Los Angeles as a city of inmates, and prisons as empire.
prisons.critique: The five moments were well chosen and spread across 2018-2026, but every quote began mid-sentence and broke off unfinished, so none stood alone. The Hernández quote stopped before reaching her point, the Victoria Law quote before the foster-care statistic, and the Burton quote before saying what Attica led to. Notes credited claims the quotes did not contain.

stops.note: Arun Kundnani on H. Rap Brown's late-1960s argument that Black labor had become surplus, and his warning that prison building would follow.
stops.quote: He says they don't need you anymore. You are a commodity in this country, a surplus. We were brought here to do work. There's no more work to do. … And he's talking about the beginnings of building prisons to remove people from society, because their labor is no longer needed.

stops.note: Kelly Lytle Hernández (City of Inmates) on reading mass incarceration through settler colonialism: a project of elimination as well as labor extraction.
stops.quote: It is about racial capitalism, absolutely. We are also fighting a genocide. So as Malcolm told us, they didn't bring us here to be citizens, and we got to really grapple with the fact that there is no long-term plan for Black life in this white settler society.

stops.note: Victoria Law (Resistance Behind Bars) on why incarcerated women's organizing priorities differ from men's, starting with their children.
stops.quote: A lot of times their priorities are different than their male counterparts because of the way society genders people's roles. For instance, parenting. … And when a mother goes to prison, her children are five times more likely to end up in foster care than those of incarcerated fathers.

stops.note: Orisanmi Burton links the 2025 New York prison guard strike to what he calls the 'distended Attica revolt' and the prison building that followed Attica.
stops.quote: I argue that the prison guard strike is really an important outcome and legacy of this distended Attica revolt, as I call it in my book. Because part of what happens after Attica is that there's a massive prison construction project all over New York.

stops.note: Brittany Friedman (Carceral Apartheid) on the San Quentin founders of the Black Guerrilla Family and her term 'carceral apartheid', the prison foundation of US empire.
stops.quote: And to do this, the founders accepted the most important truth of all, that lasting Black freedom could only come to pass across the world if liberation movements challenged what I term in this book as carceral apartheid, the carceral foundation of US empire domestically and internationally.

repression.intro: FBI campaigns against King, the Panthers and even high school students, and the Cold War purges that came before them.
repression.critique: The intro promised the Panthers, but no stop was about them. The Kundnani stop was a garbled auto-caption that misnamed Carmichael. The Garvin stop described a purge in a passing third-person summary, with 'CIO' misheard as 'CIL'. The quotes kept for Chard, Martin and Fountain each started mid-sentence and stopped before their point: the Chard quote ended on 'how did I come to this?' and the Fountain quote broke off mid-thought.

stops.note: In a tribute video shown at the 2010 conference, Esther Cooper Jackson recalls the McCarthy-era trials and her work defending Black leaders under attack.
stops.quote: There were many trials. I worked on in New York a committee called the Committee to Defend Negro Leadership. There were about 50 African Americans who had been under attack during the McCarthy period.

stops.note: Robyn Spencer on COINTELPRO and the Black Panther Party, arguing that repression did not only destroy the party but shaped it.
stops.quote: The depth of state political repression really had an impact on all aspects of the operation of the Black Panther Party. … It didn't just derail and destroy. It built. It molded.

stops.note: Daniel Chard (Nixon's War at Home) on the 1970s FBI reviving illegal surveillance once used against Communists, now aimed at guerrilla groups like the Black Liberation Army.
stops.quote: The FBI under director J. Edgar Hoover begins to revive illegal surveillance tactics like warrantless wiretapping and break-in that had been used earlier against the Communist Party but actually banned during the mid-60s by Hoover.

stops.note: Lerone Martin (The Gospel of J. Edgar Hoover) on the FBI's campaign against Martin Luther King Jr., authorized by Attorney General Robert Kennedy.
stops.quote: The FBI got permission from Attorney General Robert Kennedy to begin this campaign on Martin Luther King Jr., and it was a campaign that was involved with all branches of government. It wasn't as if J. Edgar Hoover and the FBI went rogue.

stops.note: Aaron Fountain (High School Students United) on what nearly 2,000 FOIA requests revealed about the FBI's surveillance of high school activists.
stops.quote: So, part of this research, I submitted nearly 2,000 Freedom of Information Act requests and found out that the FBI in collaboration with local police departments and the US military intelligence monitored and undermined at least 371 high school student groups, underground newspapers, student walkouts and incidents of school violence.

schools.intro: Education as a freedom struggle: Black teachers and community control, Harlem Prep, special education tracking, and liberal resistance to desegregation in New York.
schools.critique: The 2020 stop quoted Ernest Morrell describing how his edited volume was organized, which says nothing about Harlem's schools. The other four were good moments, but every quote began mid-sentence. The special education quote cut off before saying what happened to Black children, and the Harlem Prep quote dwelt on the freedom schools rather than Harlem Prep. The intro's 'community control' rested on a single list of strategies.

stops.note: Terrenda White on Harlem parents in the 1970s-2000s demanding teachers who valued their children, in the wake of the community control movements.
stops.quote: I find the 70s up until 2000, Harlem is very interesting, where a community is also saying we want the teachers who want to teach our kids, who see beauty in them, who see their gifts, who see their talents.

stops.note: Elizabeth Todd-Breland (A Political Education) on the different strategies Black Chicagoans pursued for better schools from the 1960s on.
stops.quote: I document how Black students and teachers and parents and community organizations took different approaches to improving Black education. … So in the book, I look at movements for desegregation and community control for the establishment of independent Black institutions, particularly African centered institutions in the late 60s and early 70s.

stops.note: Christopher Bonastia (The Battle Nearer to Home) on how supposedly liberal white New Yorkers responded to segregation in their own city.
stops.quote: The title of my current book refers to supposedly liberal white New Yorkers coming to terms with segregation in their own backyards rather than hundreds of miles away in the South. … The spoiler is they were not nearly as enthusiastic about dismantling segregation in New York City.

stops.note: Keith Mayes (The Unteachables) traces the overplacement of Black children in 'educable mentally retarded' (EMR) classes to late-1960s desegregation.
stops.quote: So a lot of Black children, they don't show up in mass in white schools until the late 60s, early 70s, and so you see a lot of the young kids, Black kids who may have only been in white schools for a few years, being placed in EMR classes.

stops.note: Barry Goldenberg describes Harlem Prep's 1968-69 commencement, held on 125th Street so the community could watch the graduates.
stops.quote: It's 1968, 1969. For those who know New York City, it's Central Harlem, 125th Street. So their commencement ceremony was always on the street, outside on the block for the community to witness this brilliant Black youth getting their degree.

south.intro: Disfranchisement, police killings and the segregation scholarships that sent Southern teachers North, the organizing against Jim Crow, and how its logic outlived Brown.
south.critique: The five recordings and themes are well chosen, but four of the five quotes start mid-sentence ('but she was the leader', 'mississippi plan of 1890 because', 'who was killed in Memphis', 'of Jim Crow be dismantled'), and most stop before reaching their point. The Mississippi Plan quote describes the interracial voting that provoked the plan but never the disfranchisement itself, and the Burnham quote ends before saying what happened to George Brooks. The SNYC stop reflects organizing the intro did not mention.

stops.note: Erik McDuffie, presenting his book Sojourning for Freedom, on Esther Cooper Jackson and the Southern Negro Youth Congress, which fought Jim Crow across the South in the 1930s and 1940s.
stops.quote: She was the leader of the Southern Negro Youth Congress, which in many respects was the forebearer of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. The SNYC really did some pioneering work throughout the South during the 30s and 40s around civil rights, fighting against Jim Crow.

stops.note: Carol Anderson on the 1890 Mississippi Plan, which used the conditions left by slavery to keep Black people from voting without saying so in law.
stops.quote: And so how do you say we don't want Black folk to vote without saying it? And what they decided to do was to use the legacies of slavery, those societally imposed conditions born of hundreds of years of servitude, followed by the Black codes, followed by sharecropping.

stops.note: Margaret Burnham on George Brooks, a Black Memphis postal worker framed and killed by a police officer in 1938, one of a thousand cases her archive documents.
stops.quote: He was set up and framed by the Memphis Police Department, who accused him of socializing with a white woman. … And a white police officer who had previously killed three Black men cornered George Brooks and shot him to death.

stops.note: Crystal Sanders on rural North Carolina Black women teachers who earned master's degrees in the North in the 1940s because Southern states gave them no graduate programs.
stops.quote: And I remember saying, I believe it was to my father, something like, why did they go so far away from home? And his response was something like, do you think they had a choice?

stops.note: Deborah Archer on how the logic of Jim Crow survived the civil rights victories and reappeared in transportation, including the interstate highway system.
stops.quote: So although we saw the legal architecture of Jim Crow be dismantled, that kind of underlying logic of racial hierarchy never disappeared. And it reappeared in so many systems, including in our transportation system.

vote.intro: The century-long fight for the vote and the court cases, from Brown to Milliken, that shaped where people live and learn.
vote.critique: The Rosa Parks stop quoted the audience member's question rather than any answer, and the Brown stop was credited to Kenneth Mack, but in this transcript the speaker is the Before the Movement author, Dylan Penningroth. The Chisholm and Martha Jones quotes started mid-sentence and stopped before their point. The voting half of the unit had no stop on grassroots registration work.

stops.note: A panelist at the 2010 conference on Shirley Chisholm's 1972 presidential campaign, run mostly by volunteers on a tiny budget.
stops.quote: Basically it's an almost all volunteer run campaign on a shoestring budget. I've read somewhere that the total budget is estimated about 300,000 for her national campaign, which doesn't even buy you a 30 second TV slot these days. She had one paid campaign staffer.

stops.note: Martha S. Jones (Vanguard) on why 1920 began a new 45-year fight for Black women's votes that runs to the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
stops.quote: The short answer is that in 1920 Black women, now in partnership with Black men, have to begin a voting rights movement anew in 1920, one that will take 45 years and bring us to the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

stops.topic: Law, Courts and Civil Rights Legislation
stops.note: Dylan Penningroth (Before the Movement) on Thurgood Marshall's explanation of why the Brown team used the Clarks' doll studies: argue it like a damages case.
stops.quote: Marshall's answer was really interesting. He said, I wasn't worried about this at all. I said to the team, we have to try this case just like any other case with damages. If your car ran over me, then you would have to pay up.

stops.note: A panelist on Charles Payne's I've Got the Light of Freedom: how SNCC organizer Sam Block's persistence in Greenwood, Mississippi, turned fear into mass voter registration.
stops.quote: When Sam Block, SNCC's first Greenwood organizer, came to town, people would cross the street to avoid him. … Instead of a handful of people braving the registrar's office and facing the consequences virtually alone, hundreds of people were demanding that they be allowed to try to register to vote.

stops.topic: Law, Courts and Civil Rights Legislation
stops.note: Michelle Adams (The Containment) on the 1970 suit by Black parents against Detroit's school board that became Milliken v. Bradley.
stops.quote: In 1970, a group of Black parents sued the Detroit School Board, and what they were suing about was that the Detroit school board had been running a separate and unequal school system. The reason why that was notable is because it is Detroit.

women.intro: The series' most discussed theme: Black women as organizers, thinkers and survivors, from 1600 to the present.
women.critique: The 2010 stop quotes an editor's hopes for the anthology, which says nothing about any actual woman, and the 2022 stop quotes a general aside about MeToo instead of the Fannie Lou Hamer story it comes from. Most quotes began mid-sentence ('that it would actually produce...', 'actually was a a mixed black woman...'), and the Greene quote was abstract where the talk offered the concrete Joan Little case. The years and angles were already well spread, so the fixes are mostly in which lines get quoted.

stops.note: A panelist at the 2010 Want to Start a Revolution? conference on lawyer Flo Kennedy, a NOW founder who used Black Power to frame her feminism.
stops.quote: She's a feminist, calls herself a feminist in 1966, which is really kind of different for Black women to use the title in 1966. … But what I want to talk about is how she used Black Power to frame her understanding of feminism.

stops.note: Kali Nicole Gross on opening A Black Women's History of the United States with Isabel de Olvera, a free woman of African descent who reached New Mexico around 1600.
stops.quote: Starting with Isabel de Olvera, who actually was a mixed Black woman who came to what is now New Mexico as an explorer, she actually went through great pains to go before the courts and get the documentation to demonstrate that she was in fact a free woman.

stops.note: Keisha N. Blain on Fannie Lou Hamer's televised 1964 testimony about her beating in Winona, Mississippi, as public testimony used for resistance.
stops.quote: And in that particular moment it was an example of Hamer using public testimony as a mode of resistance and revelation. So it was one way to open up the eyes of any American who at the time might have been sleeping or just complacent.

stops.note: Patricia Romney on why she wrote about the Third World Women's Alliance: students told her there were no women of color in the women's movement.
stops.quote: And I said to them, well, what about women of color? … And they said, well, there weren't any. So that really shocked me, because I had been a member of the Third World Women's Alliance, which is the group that I write about, and we were there.

stops.note: Christina Greene (Free Joan Little) on how the 1975 Joan Little case exposed narrow rape law, juries short on women and Black men, and the racist use of the death penalty.
stops.quote: The Little case also drew attention to the narrow legal definition of rape and to the under-representation of women and Black men on juries, and it became a testimonial against the racially discriminatory use of the death penalty.

work.intro: Jobs, business, banks and tenants: the economic side of freedom, from enslaved people's markets to DC tenant organizing.
work.critique: All five moments fit the unit and span 2010-2026, but every quote began mid-sentence. Several stopped just as the speaker reached the point: Gilbert Banks before his runaround, Hill Edwards before describing enslaved people's economic lives, and Garrett-Scott on how Maggie Lena Walker taught her to do history rather than on banking. The intro promised cooperatives, which no stop covered.

stops.note: Brian Purnell on Brooklyn CORE activist Gilbert Banks, a skilled World War II veteran shut out of the construction unions in the early 1960s.
stops.quote: Gilbert Banks would go to the local union hall, say, I'm an expert diesel mechanic, I'm a World War II vet, I can repair engines, I worked on jet planes … can I get a book? And at the union hall they would say, no, you need a job first.

stops.note: Julia Rabig, co-editor of The Business of Black Power, on how Black Power groups pursued liberation through economic power and federal programs.
stops.quote: Liberation meant gaining and leveraging economic power, often in sort of unexpected ways and unexpected places. It meant expanding the elements of the Civil Rights Act, the Economic Opportunity Act, the expansion of the Small Business Administration, and other policies to foster independent economic growth.

stops.note: Justene Hill Edwards (Unfree Markets) on enslaved people in South Carolina as economic actors in the rise of American capitalism.
stops.quote: They were not merely property. Enslaved men and women were hustlers by and large. They figured out ways to make money, to earn wages. They were entrepreneurs. They traded amongst themselves, with poor whites. They even traded with their enslavers, which is something I find fascinating.

stops.note: Shennette Garrett-Scott (Banking on Freedom), who studies Maggie Lena Walker's bank, on taking Black women's business efforts seriously.
stops.quote: Of course it's very easy to find the fault in free enterprise and capitalism, but I still think that we shouldn't discount these efforts on the part of Black women to transform and challenge that system from within.

stops.note: Rosemary Ndubuizu on how Black women tenant activists in DC were told their demands were unrealistic and that gentrification was the answer.
stops.quote: More often than not, they were told by politicians and sometimes their landlords … that their demands for equitable investment in welfare were unrealistic and that instead gentrification was a better political response to Black urban poverty and general working class families of color.

world.intro: Freedom struggles that crossed borders: anticolonial thinkers, Panthers in Algeria, Africa solidarity and Black movements in the Pacific.
world.critique: The intro promises Panthers in Algeria and Africa solidarity, but no stop delivers either: the Panther stop is a general statement of Third World solidarity, and the 2026 stop is Sam Klug introducing his book title. The Du Bois stop quoted Paul Ortiz's setup about voting rather than Du Bois's anti-imperialist words, and the Getachew and Swan quotes began mid-sentence with misheard place names ('wanawatu').

stops.note: A panelist on Eldridge Cleaver's flight to Algeria and the Black Panther Party's international section based there.
stops.quote: But Cleaver's flight really opened a new phase in the Panthers' internationalism. They created an international section in Algeria. Many other activists joined him there. He did a lot of traveling. And from Algeria, the Panthers' international base really, really flourished.

stops.note: Paul Ortiz reads W.E.B. Du Bois's 1928 NAACP convention speech tying Black voting rights to the fight against US imperialism.
stops.quote: The American ballot must be reestablished on a real basis of intelligence and character. Only in such way can this nation face the tremendous problems before it … the problem of imperialism and the emancipation of Haiti, Nicaragua, Cuba, the Philippines, Hawaii from the government of American banks.

stops.note: Adom Getachew (Worldmaking after Empire) on interwar Black anticolonial critics who saw empire as unequal integration and racial hierarchy, not only foreign rule.
stops.quote: I try to show that in the interwar period a wide variety of anti-colonial critics, Black anti-colonial critics, developed a conception of empire as a structure of unequal integration and racial hierarchy.

stops.note: Quito Swan (Pasifika Black) on archives of Black anticolonial movements across Melanesia and Oceania that connected to wider Black struggles.
stops.quote: So in moving around Oceania, I came across number of insurgent archives that really told this much broader story of Black anti-colonial movements across Vanuatu, Fiji, New Caledonia, Papua New Guinea, Australia, New Zealand, very much Melanesian movement, and it intersected with larger Black struggles.

stops.note: Martha Biondi (We Are Internationalists) on the anti-apartheid divestment movement that won US sanctions on South Africa over Reagan's veto in 1986.
stops.quote: Activists pressured municipal and state officials as well as corporations to divest from South Africa. They succeeded in winning congressional sanctions in 1986 over the veto of then President Ronald Reagan, who was a great friend to the apartheid regime. This historic victory accelerated the downfall of apartheid.
